---
title: 'Exercise 3: Customising colour aesthetics'
output: html_document
---


```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# No need to run this chunk unless you're "knitting"
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE,
                      comment= NA,
                      warning = FALSE,
                      message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 6)
```

Load `tidyverse` package using the `library` function.

```{r}
# Load tidyverse
library(tidyverse)
```

Load our data.

```{r}
# Load the data
d_blomkvist <- read_csv("../../data/blomkvist.csv")

# Remove missing category for smoker and missing values for rt
d_blomkvist <- drop_na(d_blomkvist, smoker, rt_hand_d)
```

We will start with a plot that has enough ink to make changes visible. Add facets will allow you to see differences in the strips.


```{r}
# Make sure the strip text is informative
d_blomkvist <- mutate(d_blomkvist, meds_cat = str_c("medication: ", meds_cat))

plot_rt <- ggplot(d_blomkvist, aes(x = age, y = rt_hand_d, colour = smoker)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~meds_cat) +
  labs(x = "Age in years", y = "Mean reaction time in msecs")

plot_rt
```
You can manually change the `theme` properties or use existing ones. For example, run the following code. We'll compare the plots using `patchwork`. Complete the missing bits in the code


```{r fig.width=10}
# Load package
library(patchwork)

# Create same plot with different themes
plot_bw <- --- + theme_bw() + labs(subtitle = "theme_bw")
plot_classic <- plot_rt + theme_classic() + labs(subtitle = "---")
plot_clean <- plot_rt + theme_---() + labs(subtitle = "theme_clean")
plot_light <- plot_rt + theme_light() + labs(subtitle = "theme_light")

# Combine all four plots
plot_bw + plot_classic + --- + plot_light

```

When you type `theme_` and you will see a drop-down list with all themes available in your environment. If you load `ggthemes` you will find even more themes to choose from. The name of the package a theme comes from is listed next to the drop-down list when you type `theme_` (after loading `ggthemes`).

```{r}
# Load package
library(ggthemes)

# Add a ggthemes theme
plot_rt + theme_---()
```
Lo and behold, there is even a `theme_tufte()`.


All themes allow you to change the base font size (default size varies). Choose a theme that you like and change the base size to 14

```{r}
plot_rt + theme_---(base_size = ---)
```

`ggplot2` allows a lot of flexibility with editing themes. In other words there are too many options to remember. The general strategy for editing themes is to first add the `theme()` function. With the cursor inside the parentheses you will the available options. There are still many. Lets explore options that I frequently change, the options starting with `axis`, `legend`, `strip`, `panel`.

`axis` allows you to change aspects of the axes, including lines, tickets, text and title for each axis or both together. For example you can increase the font size of both titles without changing the font size of other aspects of the plot. If you only want to change the font size of the x axis you'd use `axis.title.x` instead.

```{r}
plot_rt + theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 17))
```

`legend` allows you to change aspects of the title such as title, keys, location, orientation. For example if I want the legend to be positioned on the top of plot I can set `legend.position` to "top" (other options are "bottom", "right", "left") and I can use `legend.justification` to move it to the right or left. Positioning the legend on the top gives you more plotting space when you visulisation appears on an A4 page or in any situation when your horizontal space is more limited than your vertical space (not on slides).

```{r}
plot_rt + theme(legend.position = "top",
                legend.justification = "right")
```

Grid lines can be distracting in plots, especially with dark gridlines on white backgrounds. You can remove grid lines using `panel.grid`. For example if we want to remove only the minor grid lines, you can do the following.

```{r}
plot_rt + 
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The text above each panel appears in "strips". You can change things like the colour used, the text, the frame, their position etc. For example, I can remove the background altogether.

```{r}
plot_rt + 
  theme(strip.background = element_blank())
```

Combine options in the following code. I'm not saying that the result is pretty, it's just about combining skills.

```{r}
plot_rt + 
  theme(legend.position = "---", # should be on the bottom
        legend.justification = "---", # should be left
        ---, # remove all grid lines
        ---) #  make the strip text bold and red: for help check ?element.text

```

You can define themes from scratch but often it is easier to modify existing themes that already possess the properties you want. In fact, I can create my own theme:

```{r}
theme_roeser <- theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.justification = "right", 
        panel.border = element_rect())
```

and apply it to my plot.

```{r}
plot_rt + theme_roeser
```

I can also go ahead and set my theme as default to make visualisations appear in my style.


```{r}
# Set theme
theme_set(theme_roeser)

# Print plot again
plot_rt
```

Create your own theme. Include what you please but change the default settings of the following:

- location of the legend
- any text property (size, face, angle)
- strips (text, border, colour, etc)
